summary.text: Coral bleaching is when corals turn white after losing their symbiotic algae and photosynthetic pigments.
Under stress such as abnormal heat or strong light, the coral expels or consumes the algae that supply up to 90 percent of its energy, so it may starve.
Rising ocean temperatures from climate change are the leading cause, and mass bleaching has grown sharply more frequent and severe since the early 1980s.

items.prompt: A diver sees a coral that has turned ghostly white. What has happened to it?

options.label: It has lost the algae living in its tissues
It has been coated with salt crystals
It has grown a fresh outer shell
Its skeleton has dissolved away

items.explain: Bleaching is the loss of the symbiotic algae and their pigments that give coral its colour, leaving it pale or white.

items.prompt: During a long marine heatwave, a bleached coral begins to starve. Why?

options.label: Fish eat all the plankton it feeds on
Warm water dissolves the food in its gut
Its polyps close up and stop feeding
It has lost the partners that made most of its food

items.explain: Zooxanthellae provide up to 90 percent of the coral's energy through photosynthesis, so after expelling them the coral may starve.

items.prompt: A heatwave hits two reefs. Which one is more likely to have been badly affected?

options.label: A deep reef in cool, fast-moving water
A reef swept by strong ocean currents
A shallow reef in warm, still water
A reef with heavy waves breaking on it

items.explain: Reefs in warm, shallow water with low water flow have been more affected than reefs in areas with higher water flow.

items.prompt: A short burst of heat bleaches a coral, then the water cools. What must happen for the coral to recover?

options.label: It must grow an entirely new skeleton
Its algae must move back in and restart photosynthesis
It must shed every remaining algal cell
It must move to deeper, darker water

items.explain: To recover, zooxanthellae have to re-enter the coral polyps' tissues and restart photosynthesis.

items.prompt: Under mild stress, some corals turn bright blue, pink or purple instead of white. What causes these colours?

options.label: Extra algae crowding into the tissues
Dyes from pollution soaking into them
Sunburn on the exposed coral surface
The coral's own pigments staying or increasing

items.explain: This colourful bleaching comes from the continued or increased presence of the coral cells' own pigment molecules.

items.prompt: Bleached coral on a reef starves to death and decays. What happens to the reef afterwards?

options.label: New coral quickly regrows on the old skeletons
Algae take over the skeletons, which erode in time
The skeletons turn back into living coral
Nothing changes, since the skeletons last forever

items.explain: Algae take over the leftover skeletons and block coral regrowth, and eventually the skeletons erode and the reef structure collapses.

paragraphs.heading: Corals turning white
paragraphs.text: Coral bleaching is when corals go white because they lose the algae they live in partnership with, along with the pigments used for photosynthesis. Changes in water temperature, light, saltiness or nutrients can all set it off. A bleached coral is under stress, more likely to starve or fall ill, and at risk of dying.

paragraphs.heading: A partnership under strain
paragraphs.text: Reef corals depend on zooxanthellae, single-celled organisms that live inside coral tissue and give it its colour. Using photosynthesis, they supply the coral with nutrients, which matters a great deal in clear tropical water that is poor in nutrients. In return, the coral gives them the carbon dioxide and ammonium they need. These partners can meet up to 90 percent of a coral's energy needs.

paragraphs.heading: How bleaching happens
paragraphs.text: Unusually warm or cool water, strong light and even some microbial diseases can break the partnership down. To survive in the short term, the coral polyp eats or expels its zooxanthellae, and it turns pale or fully white. Under mild stress some corals turn bright blue, pink, purple or yellow instead, because their own pigments stay or increase. Without its partners the coral may begin to starve, and the longer the bad conditions last, the lower its chances.

paragraphs.heading: Recovery or collapse
paragraphs.text: To recover, zooxanthellae have to move back into the coral's tissue and start photosynthesizing again. If the polyps starve to death instead, they decay and leave behind their calcium carbonate skeletons. Algae then take over those skeletons and stop new coral from growing. Over time the skeletons erode and the reef falls apart.

paragraphs.heading: Warming seas
paragraphs.text: The leading cause is rising ocean temperature driven by climate change. Local triggers cause local bleaching, but the large-scale events of recent years have been set off by global warming. Marine heatwaves caused by El Niño are among the main causes of widespread bleaching and coral death. In 2022 the IPCC reported that mass bleaching had become sharply more frequent and severe worldwide since the early 1980s.

paragraphs.heading: Recent events
paragraphs.text: The Great Barrier Reef had its first major bleaching in 1998, and three events followed between 2016 and 2020. In 2016 alone, bleaching killed 29 to 50 percent of that reef's coral. In April 2024, NOAA confirmed that the world was in its fourth and largest global bleaching event. From January 2023 to September 2025, bleaching-level heat reached about 84.4% of the world's reef area, and bleaching was recorded in at least 83 countries and territories.
